title: Total mercury exposure in early pregnancy has no adverse association with scholastic ability of the offspring particularly if the mother eats fish.
ehr_evidence: The Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (ALSPAC) aimed to study all births to women resident in a geographic area (Avon) in the UK, whose expected date of delivery lay between the 1st April 1991 and 31st December 1992. (Data source is a prospective birth cohort with questionnaires and biospecimen assays, not EHR.)
summary: Prospective birth cohort study assessing the association between prenatal total blood mercury levels and offspring scholastic abilities, with stratification by maternal fish consumption.
key_findings: After adjustment, no significant associations were found between prenatal total blood mercury and any of the 15 scholastic test outcomes (all p > 0.05).

Stratified analysis revealed a significant interaction with maternal fish consumption: children of non-fish-eating mothers showed negative associations between mercury and mathematics/science reasoning scores, whereas children of fish-eating mothers showed positive associations.
No statistically significant differences were observed between boys and girls (data not shown).
captured_features: offspring scholastic test scores (reading, spelling, phoneme, mathematics, science)
demographic and lifestyle covariates (maternal age, parity, education, housing, smoking, alcohol, breastfeeding, stress, family adversity)
population: children born in Avon, UK (1991–1992), followed into childhood and adolescence (ages 7–13)
exposure_domain: prenatal mercury exposure and maternal fish consumption
limitations: notable attrition bias with excess drop-out from young parents, smokers, and lower socioeconomic groups
relatively small sample size of children whose mothers did not eat fish
single first-trimester blood draw may not reflect mercury levels later in pregnancy
